title: The Riverfront Stroll
technique: Left hand strides between a low bass note and mid-range chords on the off-beats. Keep the tempo relaxed and the melody singing; accuracy matters more than speed.
body: The Riverfront Stroll is a complete ragtime piano song in C major, in 2/4 time at 100 beats per minute, running 32 bars in A-A-B-A form across 4 sections. Its mood is bright syncopation over a steady march-like bass. The A sections move through tonic, subdominant, tonic, dominant seventh, while the contrasting section changes the harmonic color before the form returns home. This is an original rag built on public-domain ragtime forms: the classic rag, the cakewalk and the two-step. It is written in the style of the classic-rag era, but it is an original realization, not a copy of any existing rag and not attributed to any composer. title: The Ragtime Picnic
technique: Left hand strides between a low bass note and mid-range chords on the off-beats. Keep the tempo relaxed and the melody singing; accuracy matters more than speed.
body: The Ragtime Picnic is a complete ragtime piano song in F major, in 2/4 time at 96 beats per minute, running 32 bars in A-A-B-A form across 4 sections. Its mood is bright syncopation over a steady march-like bass. The A sections move through tonic, subdominant, tonic, dominant seventh, while the contrasting section changes the harmonic color before the form returns home. This is an original rag built on public-domain ragtime forms: the classic rag, the cakewalk and the two-step. It is written in the style of the classic-rag era, but it is an original realization, not a copy of any existing rag and not attributed to any composer. To play it, keep the left hand steady and unhurried while the right hand sings above it: striding bass and chords in the left hand Practice it first hands separately, then together at half tempo, and only then at full tempo, listening for clean releases between chords so no harmony blurs into the next.

title: The Old Piano Roll Parade
technique: Left hand plays a low bass note answered by mid-range chord blocks. Keep the tempo relaxed and the melody singing; accuracy matters more than speed.
body: The Old Piano Roll Parade is a complete ragtime piano song in Bb major, in 2/4 time at 100 beats per minute, running 32 bars in A-A-B-A form across 4 sections. Its mood is bright syncopation over a steady march-like bass. The A sections move through tonic, subdominant, tonic, dominant seventh, while the contrasting section changes the harmonic color before the form returns home. This is an original rag built on public-domain ragtime forms: the classic rag, the cakewalk and the two-step. It is written in the style of the classic-rag era, but it is an original realization, not a copy of any existing rag and not attributed to any composer. To play it, keep the left hand steady and unhurried while the right hand sings above it: bass note plus chord blocks in the left hand Practice it first hands separately, then together at half tempo, and only then at full tempo, listening for clean releases between chords so no harmony blurs into the next.

title: Ragtime at the Riverboat Landing
technique: Left hand plays a low bass note answered by mid-range chord blocks. Shape the phrasing in two-bar breaths and let the syncopation sit inside the beat, never ahead of it.
body: Ragtime at the Riverboat Landing is a complete ragtime piano song in E major, in 4/4 time at 116 beats per minute, running 32 bars in A-B-A-B form across 4 sections. Its mood is bright syncopation over a steady march-like bass. The A sections move through tonic, subdominant, tonic, dominant seventh, while the contrasting section changes the harmonic color before the form returns home. This is an original rag built on public-domain ragtime forms: the classic rag, the cakewalk and the two-step. It is written in the style of the classic-rag era, but it is an original realization, not a copy of any existing rag and not attributed to any composer. To play it, keep the left hand steady and unhurried while the right hand sings above it: bass note plus chord blocks in the left hand Practice it first hands separately, then together at half tempo, and only then at full tempo, listening for clean releases between chords so no harmony blurs into the next.

title: The Corner Store Rag
technique: Left hand strides between a low bass note and mid-range chords on the off-beats. Shape the phrasing in two-bar breaths and let the syncopation sit inside the beat, never ahead of it.
body: The Corner Store Rag is a complete ragtime piano song in C major, in 2/4 time at 100 beats per minute, running 32 bars in A-A-B-A form across 4 sections. Its mood is bright syncopation over a steady march-like bass. The A sections move through tonic, subdominant, tonic, dominant seventh, while the contrasting section changes the harmonic color before the form returns home. This is an original rag built on public-domain ragtime forms: the classic rag, the cakewalk and the two-step. It is written in the style of the classic-rag era, but it is an original realization, not a copy of any existing rag and not attributed to any composer. To play it, keep the left hand steady and unhurried while the right hand sings above it: striding bass and chords in the left hand Practice it first hands separately, then together at half tempo, and only then at full tempo, listening for clean releases between chords so no harmony blurs into the next.

body: Afternoon at the Bandstand is a complete ragtime piano song in G major, in 4/4 time at 112 beats per minute, running 32 bars in A-A-B-A form across 4 sections. Its mood is bright syncopation over a steady march-like bass. The A sections move through tonic, subdominant, tonic, dominant seventh, while the contrasting section changes the harmonic color before the form returns home. This is an original rag built on public-domain ragtime forms: the classic rag, the cakewalk and the two-step. It is written in the style of the classic-rag era, but it is an original realization, not a copy of any existing rag and not attributed to any composer. To play it, keep the left hand steady and unhurried while the right hand sings above it: striding bass and chords in the left hand Practice it first hands separately, then together at half tempo, and only then at full tempo, listening for clean releases between chords so no harmony blurs into the next.

title: Cakewalk for a Summer Evening
technique: Left hand strides between a low bass note and mid-range chords on the off-beats. At full tempo the passagework must stay even and light; practice the fastest bars slowly until every note speaks.
body: Cakewalk for a Summer Evening is a complete ragtime piano song in D major, in 4/4 time at 116 beats per minute, running 32 bars in A-B-A-B form across 4 sections. Its mood is bright syncopation over a steady march-like bass. The A sections move through tonic, subdominant, tonic, dominant seventh, while the contrasting section changes the harmonic color before the form returns home. This is an original rag built on public-domain ragtime forms: the classic rag, the cakewalk and the two-step. It is written in the style of the classic-rag era, but it is an original realization, not a copy of any existing rag and not attributed to any composer. To play it, keep the left hand steady and unhurried while the right hand sings above it: striding bass and chords in the left hand Practice it first hands separately, then together at half tempo, and only then at full tempo, listening for clean releases between chords so no harmony blurs into the next.

title: The Trolley Car Two-Step
technique: Left hand strides between a low bass note and mid-range chords on the off-beats. At full tempo the passagework must stay even and light; practice the fastest bars slowly until every note speaks.
body: The Trolley Car Two-Step is a complete ragtime piano song in Bb major, in 2/4 time at 100 beats per minute, running 32 bars in A-A-B-A form across 4 sections. Its mood is bright syncopation over a steady march-like bass. The A sections move through tonic, subdominant, tonic, dominant seventh, while the contrasting section changes the harmonic color before the form returns home. This is an original rag built on public-domain ragtime forms: the classic rag, the cakewalk and the two-step. It is written in the style of the classic-rag era, but it is an original realization, not a copy of any existing rag and not attributed to any composer. To play it, keep the left hand steady and unhurried while the right hand sings above it: striding bass and chords in the left hand Practice it first hands separately, then together at half tempo, and only then at full tempo, listening for clean releases between chords so no harmony blurs into the next.

title: Ragtime on a Rainy Sunday
technique: Left hand plays a low bass note answered by mid-range chord blocks. At full tempo the passagework must stay even and light; practice the fastest bars slowly until every note speaks.
body: Ragtime on a Rainy Sunday is a complete ragtime piano song in Eb major, in 4/4 time at 112 beats per minute, running 32 bars in A-A-B-A form across 4 sections. Its mood is bright syncopation over a steady march-like bass. The A sections move through tonic, subdominant, tonic, dominant seventh, while the contrasting section changes the harmonic color before the form returns home. This is an original rag built on public-domain ragtime forms: the classic rag, the cakewalk and the two-step. It is written in the style of the classic-rag era, but it is an original realization, not a copy of any existing rag and not attributed to any composer. To play it, keep the left hand steady and unhurried while the right hand sings above it: bass note plus chord blocks in the left hand Practice it first hands separately, then together at half tempo, and only then at full tempo, listening for clean releases between chords so no harmony blurs into the next.

title: The Grand Parade Rag
technique: Left hand strides between a low bass note and mid-range chords on the off-beats. At full tempo the passagework must stay even and light; practice the fastest bars slowly until every note speaks.
body: The Grand Parade Rag is a complete ragtime piano song in A major, in 2/4 time at 96 beats per minute, running 32 bars in A-A-B-A form across 4 sections. Its mood is bright syncopation over a steady march-like bass. The A sections move through tonic, subdominant, tonic, dominant seventh, while the contrasting section changes the harmonic color before the form returns home. This is an original rag built on public-domain ragtime forms: the classic rag, the cakewalk and the two-step. It is written in the style of the classic-rag era, but it is an original realization, not a copy of any existing rag and not attributed to any composer. To play it, keep the left hand steady and unhurried while the right hand sings above it: striding bass and chords in the left hand Practice it first hands separately, then together at half tempo, and only then at full tempo, listening for clean releases between chords so no harmony blurs into the next.

title: The Riverboat Jubilee Rag
technique: Left hand strides between a low bass note and mid-range chords on the off-beats. At full tempo the passagework must stay even and light; practice the fastest bars slowly until every note speaks.
body: The Riverboat Jubilee Rag is a complete ragtime piano song in E major, in 4/4 time at 116 beats per minute, running 32 bars in A-B-A-B form across 4 sections. Its mood is bright syncopation over a steady march-like bass. The A sections move through tonic, subdominant, tonic, dominant seventh, while the contrasting section changes the harmonic color before the form returns home. This is an original rag built on public-domain ragtime forms: the classic rag, the cakewalk and the two-step. It is written in the style of the classic-rag era, but it is an original realization, not a copy of any existing rag and not attributed to any composer. To play it, keep the left hand steady and unhurried while the right hand sings above it: striding bass and chords in the left hand Practice it first hands separately, then together at half tempo, and only then at full tempo, listening for clean releases between chords so no harmony blurs into the next.
